## Overview

**SA24204150** is an R package developed for the *Statistical Computing* course.
The package focuses on two aspects:

1. **Survival analysis and model evaluation**, including

   * estimation of the censoring survival function,
   * Cox-model-based survival prediction,
   * IPCW Brier score evaluation;

2. **Algorithmic subset construction**, implemented using both R and C++ (via the R package *Rcpp*).

Specifically, the package contains three R functions for survival analysis,
namely *G.hat*, *S.hat*, and *bs*, as well as two Rcpp functions,
*generate_subsetsC* and *generate_nested_subsetsC*,
which are designed to efficiently generate subsets commonly used in greedy or sequential modeling procedures.

---

## Subset construction using Rcpp

Subset generation is a fundamental building block in many statistical learning
and model selection algorithms.
In R, such operations are often implemented using high-level functions such as
*combn*, which can be computationally expensive for large input sizes.
In this package, two subset-generation functions are implemented in C++ using *Rcpp*.

### Generating all non-empty subsets

The Rcpp function *generate_subsetsC* generates all non-empty subsets of a given set.

The source C++ code is as follows:

List generate_subsetsC(IntegerVector set) {
int n = set.size();
int total = (1 << n);
List subsets;

for (int mask = 1; mask < total; ++mask) {
IntegerVector subset;
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
if (mask & (1 << i)) {
subset.push_back(set[i]);
}
}
subsets.push_back(subset);
}
return subsets;
}

This implementation enumerates subsets using bit masking, which is both concise
and efficient.

An example usage is shown below.

library(SA25204001)
generate_subsetsC(1:3)

---

### Generating nested subsets

In many greedy algorithms, only *nested* subsets are required.
The function *generate_nested_subsetsC* generates the sequence

[
{1}, {1,2}, \ldots, {1,\ldots,n}.
]

The corresponding C++ code is:

List generate_nested_subsetsC(IntegerVector set) {
int n = set.size();
List subsets(n);
for (int i = 0; i < n; ++i) {
subsets[i] = set[Range(0, i)];
}
return subsets;
}

An example is given below.

generate_nested_subsetsC(1:5)

---

## Survival analysis functions

In addition to subset construction, the package provides several R functions
for survival analysis and prediction.

### Estimation of the censoring survival function

The function *G.hat* computes the Kaplan–Meier estimator of the censoring survival
function, which is used for inverse probability of censoring weighting (IPCW).

The R source code is:

G.hat <- function(t, Dat) {
newDat = list()
newDat$x = Dat$x
newDat$Delta = 1 - Dat$Delta
newDat$Y = Dat$Y
fit = survfit(Surv(Y, Delta) ~ 1, data = newDat)
if (t <= fit$time[1]) {
return(1)
} else {
q = max(which(fit$time <= t))
return(fit$surv[q])
}
}

An example of using *G.hat* is shown below.

library(survival)
set.seed(123)
n <- 100
Dat <- list(
x = matrix(rnorm(n * 3), n, 3),
Y = rexp(n),
Delta = rbinom(n, 1, 0.7)
)
G.hat(0.5, Dat)

---

### Cox-model-based survival prediction

The function *S.hat* fits a sequence of Cox proportional hazards models and
predicts survival probabilities at a fixed time point.

h <- 2
newX <- Dat$x
newX_test <- matrix(rnorm(50 * 3), 50, 3)

Dat_test <- list(
x = newX_test,
Y = rexp(50),
Delta = rbinom(50, 1, 0.7)
)

res <- S.hat(
newX = newX,
newX_test = newX_test,
ns = n,
ns_test = 50,
t = 0.5,
Datas = Dat,
Datas_test = Dat_test
)

dim(res$S)

---

### IPCW Brier score

Finally, the function *bs* computes the IPCW Brier score at a fixed time point.

bs(
newX = newX,
newX_test = newX_test,
ns = n,
ns_test = 50,
t = 0.5,
Dat = Dat,
Dat_test = Dat_test,
k = 1
)

---

## Conclusion

This vignette demonstrates the usage of all major functions provided in the
package **SA25204001**.
The Rcpp functions offer efficient subset generation for algorithmic procedures,
while the R functions focus on survival analysis and model evaluation.
Together, they illustrate how R and C++ can be combined effectively in
statistical computing.
